It’s been… I’d say a couple of months now that I just haven’t felt like myself. Ever since everything started changing with my living situation and my health, I feel on edge most of the time. I wake up already tense, like my shoulders are up by my ears, and my mind starts racing before I’m even out of bed—worrying about money, my blood pressure, being alone in the house, you name it.

I’ve always been a bit of a worrier, even back when I was on the ward, but this feels different. There’s this constant nervousness, like I’ve had too much coffee, even when I haven’t. I catch myself fiddling with my hands or pacing the hallway without realizing it. When my daughter leaves after visiting, I get this panicky, knotted feeling in my stomach; I hate seeing her go, and I start imagining something happening to me and no one noticing.

I wouldn’t say I’m completely unable to enjoy things—I still watch my shows and talk to my neighbor—but there’s a heaviness there, and I get tired more easily. Some days I just sit and stare at the garden, thinking too much, feeling low and jumpy at the same time.
D020-D013_h001.question_a:
Since my husband died about two months ago, I just haven’t been myself. It really started a few weeks after the funeral. I feel on edge most of the time—kind of wired and jumpy, like I’m waiting for bad news. I catch myself pacing around the house, checking the locks, worrying something will happen to the kids or grandkids, even though they’re fine. Nights are the worst: my mind runs through every “what if,” and it takes me a long time to fall asleep.

I am sad, of course—I miss him terribly and I cry some evenings, especially when I see his chair or hear our song on the radio. But it comes and goes; there are still moments I can enjoy a phone call with my daughter or a visit from the neighbors. I’m still eating more or less normally, and I get up, bathe, pay the bills, even help out at church sometimes. I don’t feel completely weighed down or hopeless all day, every day. It just feels like I’m having a hard time adjusting since he passed, and the nervousness and worry are what bother me the most.
D020-D013_h001.question_b:
It really started after my husband died about eight months ago, but it’s gone far beyond just missing him. I wake up every day with this heavy feeling, like there’s no point. I’m sad pretty much all day, every day, and it hasn’t really lifted at all. I used to be a very involved grandmother and still volunteered at the hospital sometimes, but I’ve stopped all of that. I don’t enjoy anything anymore, not even seeing the kids.

My sleep is terrible—either I’m up half the night or I wake at 4 a.m. and can’t fall back asleep. My appetite’s gone; I’ve lost about ten pounds without trying. I move slower, and simple things like showering or making a sandwich feel like climbing a mountain. I feel useless, like I failed my husband and my family, and I keep thinking they’d be better off without me, though I haven’t made any plans.

On top of that, I’m constantly tense and on edge—jittery, worrying something bad will happen to the family. I know his death triggered this, but it feels much deeper and more constant than just reacting to the loss.

D020-D013_h002.question_a:
It really started about two months ago, after I got written up at work for a mistake on a night shift. Since then I just haven’t felt like myself. I’m not falling apart completely, but I feel…off. I’m more down than usual, kind of on edge, and it’s all tied to that incident and worrying I’ll mess up again and lose my job.

I still get out of bed, go to work, and can focus enough to do my shifts, but once I’m home I just shut down. I avoid my friends, ignore calls, and mostly stay in my apartment. My stomach’s knotty a lot, I get random headaches, and my chest feels tight when I think about going back on radar. I’m not crying all the time, my appetite’s mostly normal, and I can still sleep, though it’s a bit disrupted.

The low mood isn’t constant—some days are okay, and if work feels calmer, I actually enjoy watching games or going for a run. I don’t have thoughts of hurting myself. It just feels like I’ve been stuck in this reaction to what happened at work and can’t quite shake it.
D020-D013_h002.question_b:
It really started about three, maybe four months ago, after I got written up for a minor mistake at work. At first I thought I was just shaken up, but it’s like something in me just…shut down and never came back online.

Most days I wake up already exhausted, even if I’ve slept 9–10 hours, and honestly I’m sleeping more than that on my days off. I used to go to the gym before early shifts; now I just lie there staring at the ceiling, thinking there’s no point. I’ve pretty much stopped seeing friends and just ignore group chats. On my breaks at the tower I’ll sit alone, scrolling without really seeing anything.

I feel this heavy, constant sadness and guilt, like I’m a failure and everyone would be better off if I wasn’t around. I can’t enjoy anything I used to—flying, games, even watching sports. My concentration at work is shot; I’ll reread the same line on a strip three times to make sure I’m not missing something, and that scares me in my job. My appetite’s way down; some days I just grab coffee and maybe a snack. It hasn’t let up at all over these months—it’s just there, all the time.

I’m more down than usual, kind of discouraged and tearful at times, but it seems tied to thinking about work and possibly having to lay off teachers. On weekends, if I’m with my grandchildren or busy in the garden, I can still enjoy myself and feel like my old self for stretches.

I get this constant knot in my stomach and my mind keeps looping through “what if” scenarios—what if the board blames me, what if the scores drop. I’m more on edge, irritable with my husband, and having trouble falling asleep because I’m replaying meetings in my head. My appetite is a bit off, but I’m not losing a lot of weight, and I still get out of bed every morning and go to school. I’m not completely hopeless, and I’m not thinking about hurting myself.

If this whole situation resolved, I have a sense this heaviness and worry would ease up. Before all this started, I was pretty stable emotionally.
D020-D013_h024.question_b:
It really started about six months ago, after the district announced major budget cuts. At first I thought I was just stressed, but it’s gone way beyond that. I wake up every day feeling this heavy emptiness, like there’s no point. I used to love being at school, greeting the kids, planning programs—now I have to force myself to get out of bed and go in. Most days I feel on the verge of tears for no obvious reason.

I worry constantly about everything—the teachers, the test scores, even little things at home—but the worry just circles in my head and keeps me up at night. My sleep is awful: I either wake at 3 or 4 a.m. and can’t fall back asleep, or just lie there tense. My appetite’s dropped; I’ve lost interest in food and a few pounds without trying.

I don’t enjoy anything anymore, even time with my husband or our grandchildren. I feel guilty, like I’m failing everyone at school and at home. I move more slowly, can’t concentrate in meetings, and my mind goes blank when I try to read. This hasn’t let up at all, it’s every day, all day.

D020-D013_h025.question_both:
It’s been… I don’t know, a few months now since everything really went off the rails after the last big case and the fallout with my ex. Since then I just haven’t been myself.

I’m angrier and more reckless than I’ve ever been. I’ve gotten into a couple of shouting matches that almost turned into physical fights—one outside the courthouse, another in a parking lot. I’ve been driving way too fast, cutting people off, blowing through yellow lights like I don’t care what happens. Part of me almost doesn’t.

I’ve started doing things that are just… out of character. I keyed someone’s car after an argument over a parking space, and a few weeks later I smashed a side mirror in a garage because the guy “looked at me wrong.” I know that sounds ridiculous for a man my age, and definitely for someone in my profession.

On top of that, I feel low a lot of the time—tired, unmotivated, not enjoying the things I used to. I still get myself to work and handle my cases, but it feels like I’m moving through molasses. I can’t tell if this is me just reacting badly to everything that’s happened, or if it’s something more.
D020-D013_h025.question_a:
About four months ago my ex-wife finalized the divorce and moved in with her new partner. Up until then I was functioning fine, working long hours at the firm like always. Within a few weeks of the papers being signed, I started feeling low and irritable most days—sad, angry, kind of empty—but it comes and goes. I still get some enjoyment out of work and watching sports, and my appetite and sleep are off but not completely shot.

What worries me more is how I’ve been acting. I’ve been driving way too fast, blowing through yellow lights, even had a couple of close calls. Two months ago I got into a shouting match in a bar and it nearly turned into a fight, which is not like me at all. I’ve also punched a hole in a wall in my condo after an argument with my son on the phone.

These changes really started after the divorce; before that I wasn’t like this. I’m not constantly down all day, every day, and I’m still going to work and handling cases, but I feel on edge and out of control. If this divorce mess settles, I’m hoping this will, too.
D020-D013_h025.question_b:
It’s been a little over two months now, and it’s like something just… shut down. The divorce was finalized in October, and at first I thought I was just reacting to that, but this feels different. I wake up every morning around 4 a.m., exhausted, but I can’t fall back asleep. I used to enjoy work, arguing cases, mentoring the juniors. Now I sit in my office staring at files, unable to concentrate for more than a few minutes, and then I just give up and go home. 

I don’t really feel pleasure in anything anymore—no golf, no dinners out, nothing. My appetite’s gone; I’ve lost about 15 pounds without trying. Most days I’m either on the couch or pacing the apartment, feeling this heavy, constant guilt, like I failed as a husband and a father, and honestly as a lawyer too. 

I’ve started driving way too fast at night, almost hoping something will happen, and got into a shouting match in a parking lot that nearly became a fight, which is not like me at all. I think about death a lot—wondering if everyone would be better off without me—though I haven’t made a specific plan.
